i ntroduction
Clustering techniques fall into two major categories, hierarchical techniques and optimiza-
tion or partitioned techniques.
h ierarchical t echniques
Hierarchical clustering can be broken down into two major categories agglomerative methods
and divisive methods. A procedure for forming agglomerative hierarchical groups of mutu-
ally exclusive subsets based on the premise that the greatest amount of information, as indi-
cated by the objective function, is available when a set of n members is ungrouped. The first
step is to select and combine the two subsets out of the n possible subsets which would pro-
duce the least impairment of the optimum value of the objective function, while reducing
the number of subsets to n − 1. These n − 1 subsets are then examined to identify which two
subsets should be merged in order to obtain the optimum value of the objective function for
n − 2 subsets. This procedure is repeated until the original n members are in a single set or
group. Since the number of subsets is reduced by one at each step (n, n − 1, ... , 1), the pro-
cess is referred to as hierarchical grouping. The grouping which occurs at each step usually
results in some quantifiable loss. The functional relation used to obtain a value-reflecting
number is called the objective function. In general, an objective function may be any func-
tional relationship that an investigator selects to reflect the relative desirability of groupings.
The objective function represents loss of information and is reflected by the error sum of
squares, (known as Ward’s Method). Other examples of objective functions can include:
1. the grand sum of the squared deviations about the means of all measured charac-
teristics, people are clustered to maximize their similarity with respect to measured
characteristics,
2. the expected cross-training time in the clustering of jobs to minimize cross-training
time when personnel are reassigned according to established policies,
3. the amount of job time incorrectly described to minimize errors. When clustering job
descriptions in describing a large number of jobs with a small number of descriptions, and
4. the loss of predictive efficiency when clustering regression equations to minimize
the loss of predicted efficiency resulting from reductions in the number of regression
equations judgmental analysis (JAN).
An important concept to remember in defining the hierarchical grouping mentioned above is
that once two entities are merged, they are joined permanently and become a building block
for later merges. This is one of the key differences between the hierarchical techniques and
the optimal techniques to be discussed in the next section. Another difference between the

the entire hierarchical tree structure, they must decide at what point the best clustering has
been reached. There are many different techniques available to help the user make a selection.
Some of the more common hierarchical techniques are the nearest neighbor (single linkage)
method, the farthest neighbor (complete linkage) method, centroid method, and Ward’s method
560 n n n r e S earch Metho DS for I N for M at I o N Sy S te MS n ch apter 42
(mentioned earlier in the chapter). The basic technique for these methods is similar. However,
there are two factors that differentiate between the methods. The first factor is whether the
technique can be used with similarity measures, distance measures, or both. The second factor
is how these measures are defined, or, in Ward’s terminology, the objective function.
In divisive clustering the initial starting point is with all entities in one group. The first step is
to split the group into two subsets. Subsequent steps consist of subdividing the subsets until
each entity is a separate group. There are two classes of methods for deciding how to split
the groups. With the monothetic methods, the data points are based on binary variables and
the object is to split the data set on one of these variables so as to minimize the value of some
appropriate measure of similarity between the two groups. The splitting process, based on
other variables, continues until some criterion is reached. Examples of monothetic techniques
include association analysis and the automatic interaction detector method. The polythetic
methods are based on the values taken by all of the variables. The divisive techniques have not
gained the same popularity as the agglomerative techniques and their use is minimal.
Optimization t echniques
The basic method used by the optimization techniques is to obtain an initial partition of the
data units and then alter the cluster membership to get a better partition, i.e., until a local
optimum is found. The various methods differ as to how they arrive at an initial partition and
how they define “better” (i.e., the objective function). The techniques in this section differ
from the hierarchical techniques in two ways. First, members are allowed to change cluster
membership. So, a data point poorly classified in an early cycle can be re-classified in a later
step. Second, the number of clusters must be specified in advance. If the structure of the
data is known a priori, this is not a problem. Otherwise, two possible suggestions are to:
1. try a number of different partitions, or
2. use a hierarchical technique first to help decide upon the number of clusters.

In the k-means approach, once the initial partitions have been established, the cluster cen-
troid can be updated after each addition to the cluster (MacQueen’s method), or only after
all the points have been allocated (Forgy method and Jancey method).
The basic algorithm for MacQueen’s method is as follows:
1. Begin with an initial partition of the data units into clusters (any of the methods men-
tioned earlier will work).
2. Take each data unit in sequence and compute the distances to all cluster centroids; if
the nearest centroid is not that of the data unit’s parent cluster, then reassign the data
unit and update the centroids of the losing and gaining clusters.
3. Repeat step 2 until convergence is achieved; that is, continue until a full cycle
through the data set fails to cause any changes in cluster membership.
The basic algorithm for Forgy’s method is to:
1. Begin with any desired initial configuration. Go to step 2 if beginning with a set of
seed points; go to step 3 if beginning with a partition of the data units.
2. Allocate each data unit to the cluster with the nearest seed point. The seed points
remain fixed for a full cycle through the entire data set.
3. Compute new seed points as the centroids of the clusters of data units.
4. Alternate steps 2 and 3 until the process converges; that is, continue until no data
units change their cluster membership at step 2.
At this point a local optimum has been achieved. Unfortunately, there is no way to know
whether this is also the global optimum. The solution can either be accepted, or a new initial
partition can be obtained and the clusters can be re-analyzed.

43.1 i ntroduction
This chapter provides an overview of statistical software. Sketches of answers are provided
for responding to: What considerations are important in the design of a statistical software
package? What design constructs are possible? How can packages be compared? How can a
researcher select the package which best suits their needs?
In many, if not most situations, the researcher will not be able to choose from the entire array
of all available packages, but will have to select from a more limited list of the packages avail-
able. The questions above remain important, however, for choosing wisely from this limited
list and for using the selected package efficiency and effectively.
43.2 d esign c onstructs
Current statistical software packages designs are dependent upon what type of interface
is implemented. Several packages interface with relational database systems such as
ORACLE. Other packages interface with mathematical software. For instance MATLAB
is one which not only offers statistical capabilities but optimization and symbolic
manipulation. Some packages utilize visualization interfaces, which is a very useful fea-
ture for exploratory data analysis. User interfaces come in many sizes and shapes as they
have evolved from command line to graphical user interfaces to hybrid drag and drop
system interfaces.
An applications software package, in statistics or in any other area, may take one of these
four forms:
1. A set of independent programs.
2. A set of subroutines to be called by a user-generated program.
3. A single, multipurpose program.
4. An applications compiler.
The design of a package must take into account a number of considerations, including:
1. The intended application of the package (primarily the behavioral sciences, some
other area, or a number of fields).
2. The background of users (undergraduates or professional statisticians).
3. The level of experience of the users (familiarity with computers and programming).
4. The hardware the package will run on.
We now consider the four major design constructs in more detail.

43.2.1 s ets of programs
In a package of this kind, each program is complete in itself, and each performs just one statis-
tical operation on the data file: computing descriptive statistics, for example, or performing a
t-test. Each program will use the same input formatting, style of documentation, and coding
language, and some effort will also be made to standardize the output formats. The advan-
tages of such a package are these: the programs can be easily used by a nonprogrammer, and

they generally offer some flexibility of input format. In many cases, however, the user will
want to perform many analyses on a particular data file, or the same analysis on several files.
A package of individual programs is clumsy and time consuming in such situations.
43.2.2 s ets of subroutines
When the package consists of a set of subroutines, the user must write a main program to
read in the data file and call the subroutines to perform statistical analyses. This main pro-
gram will be written in a high-level language, while the subroutines will be entirely input-
free. There are several advantages to such a package
1. Statistical processing can be tailored to each job.
2. Repetitive runs of several programs can be done easily.
3. Routines not in the package can be supplied by the user.
On the other hand, a set of subroutines can be used only by someone familiar with program-
ming in the language of the subroutines; many statistical users will not have such training.
Packages of this type generally have less documentation provided than might be required by
the general user. Therefore, a high level of sophistication in computing may be required to
obtain statistical results.

43.2.3 Large, multiple-use programs
Many packages today are single, large programs and can be divided into two subcatego-
ries. In the first, the entire program, which can perform a variety of statistical and pro-
cessing tasks, is maintained in the computer’s memory. Such packages tend to occupy vast
amounts of storage, and they can require large amounts of time for I/O. They are, how-
ever, easily used by the nonprogrammer. In the second, the first section of code loaded
into main memory produces a menu of available operations, then generates calls to the
parts of the program which perform tasks the user requests, either in a specified code
or in some language prose series of statements. Only those parts of the program related
to the current tasks are maintained in memory, which can then be used more efficiently.
Such systems are well-adapted to interactive use, and some also provide tutorial sessions
in the use of the package.
43.2.4 a pplication compilers
Packages of this type are, in fact, programming languages in which statistical tasks, or large
steps in statistical tasks, are initiated by single statements in the language. They are useful to
the researcher who wants to perform a nonstandard analysis quickly, but they again require

that the user be a competent programmer. Implementation of a statistical applications
compiler can be accomplished with a functional paradigm programming language.
43.3 p roblem a reas
Many, if not most statistical packages, now in wide use were written by programmers
rather than statisticians. Today many package systems are constructed in modules
and adapted to current technology but with minimal documentation. These and other
conditions have led to the following problem areas in the design and use of statistical
packages:
1. Statistical packages are often misunderstood, inefficiently used, even misused.
The ease with which some packages can be used may encourage the unwary to apply the
analyses in the package to situations and data inconsistent with the techniques available. For
example, assume that a group of values has come from a normally distributed population
when this has not been established. Documentation should show not only how to cause the
analyses to be performed but also the situations to which the analyses are applicable, the
assumptions on which the techniques are based, and the conclusions that can be drawn. This
information should be available not only in the written documentation of the package but
also in online tutorial help sessions.
2. Overly stringent requirements of system hardware or software.
Some packages are written for specific architectural platforms, and can be used only with
difficulty, if at all, on any other platform. Some require specialized devices, a plotter, for

example, that may not be available.
3. Lack of transportability.
It should be possible to execute a package on a wide variety of architectures, par-
ticularly since hardware/software changes at computer facilities occur with surprising
frequency. Acquisition of a new machine should not render all purchased software
unusable. Import/export facilities are extremely important components needed in cur-
rent applications. For instance, Excel has been widely used for entry and management
of data.
4. Inflexible and complicated user interfaces.
In some earlier packages, the statements used to control the operation of the package seemed
almost intentionally obscure, with stringent requirements for the placement of instructions
on each line and instructions which, at first glance, seem arbitrary sequences of characters.
Graphical user interfaces greatly enhance the usability of a package and should be easily
accessible to those who use it. In particular, English-like words should be used, and their
placement on the lines should not be overly critical.

43.4 d esirable p ackage f eatures
It is obvious that the single most desirable characteristic of any package of programs is ease
of use; the two primary areas here are formatting input of the data file and instructing the
package to perform the desired tasks. A package that does not allow direct, easily understood
operation in these areas can be more of an impediment than an aid. Other useful character-
istics of a statistical program package are:
1. An interactive process to generate successive models, with each model a better
approximation of the situation represented by the data. Graphical displays are
desirable here.
2. An English-like command structure.
3. Intelligible error messages during execution to avoid dependence on the documentation.
4. Results in English sentences whenever possible, rather than just tables of values.
5. The ability to generate new values based on existing values.
6. The inclusion of a end-user friendly graphical user interface.
7. Hardcopy documentation and online help sessions/tutorials showing examples of data
files, runs using the package, and interpretation of results.
8. The ability to manipulate data files.
This last characteristic deserves further comment. In addition to sorting of files, the attach-
ment labels to variables, and the selection of particular cases, it is also often useful to invert
a file, that is, to rearrange the records in a new order based on the values of a particular
variable.

44.1 i ntroduction
A college major in computer science would classify computational complexity as a theoretical
or foundational topic. The same student would also classify data structures or design of algo-
rithms as applied computer science studies. What is the difference between theoretical and
applied studies? The student’s perception probably leads them in this direction based upon
operationally defining applied areas of study as those studies being real-world-solutions to
real-world-problems. At the same time, the student probably perceives areas of study that
expand knowledge in the field as theoretical.
However, appearances can be deceptive. Many of the topics covered in computational
complexity classes evolved from real-world problems, such as the need for determining if a
problem is solvable with a specific architecture. On the other hand, attempting to solve real-
world-problems can help one to discover new knowledge and is, therefore, defined as usually
theoretical. There appears to be a non-empty intersection between theoretical and applied
domains. Possibly it is better to think of application as a catalyst for expanding knowledge in
the field and theoretical studies as preparation for application.
44 .2 s ample s tudy
The study discussed here is a cognitive-map-based approach to the coordination of distrib-
uted cooperative agents available online at http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/.
Ternary logic is employed, through the use of negative-positive-neural logic (NPN), in this
study to allow for response to stimuli by representative states of “agreement, disagreement,
or maybe.” Using NPN components, the researchers have has constructed a pooled cognitive
map that is derived from a network of cognitive maps. Each node in the network represents
either an Artificial Intelligent (AI) agent’s or a human agent’s cognitive map; it represents the
agent’s positive to negative reactions to stimuli. The network is implemented in the LISP and
C programming languages.
A typical application for this system consists of gathering a group of both AI and human experts
on a domain area to consider a specific problem. The system, called D-POOL, commences
with several of the local nodes, broadcasting the problem statement throughout the network.
Next a determination of the identity of valid experts as well as pooling the cognitive maps, is
derived from their assigned groups. Finally, all the originally chosen local nodes, or experts,
have their cognitive map stored. When the problem of interest is presented to each expert

cognitive map. This map represents the knowledge mapping derived by coordination of dis-
tributed cooperative human and AI experts, still remaining in the study thereby formulating
a solution to the problem. DPOOL generates cooperative, or compromised, problem solving

For the article presented in the previous section, the hypothesis tested is:
Coherence and coordination can be achieved with a set of autonomous intelligent agents,

without centralized control or viewpoints in a distributed environment, through agent actions
based upon cognitive integrity, transparency, and simplicity.
The basic need for this hypothesis test includes the following issues:
n Each node, either an expert system or human expert, is represented as a cognitive
map system. A systematic approach to problem solving is taken to construct a pooled
cognitive map for representing the pooled knowledge and reasoning techniques
contributed by the participating experts. Note that this involves fuzzy reasoning.
n Enforcing cognitive integrity enables the agents to derive a sufficient “big picture” of
the distributed environment, or the composite and/or derivative view.
n Enforcing both cognitive transparency and simplicity ensures that the “picture” given
to each agent is clearly understandable, modifiable, and transmittable.
We are left with asking what criteria could be used to determine whether a theory is an
adequate one. A number of such criteria can be found in the literature. However, it must be
recognized that their application is a matter of rational analysis and can give only a general
indication of theoretical adequacy. This theory from the field of study in distributed artificial
intelligence passes the following criteria for testing the adequacy of the latter hypothesis test:
c riteria for adequacy testing theory
n Testability — A theory should lead to deductions that can be credited or discredited
by empirical test.
n Consistency — A theory should be free from internal contradiction or be logically
consistent.
n Scope — A theory should account for a relatively wide range of data.
n Predictive power — A theory should provide a basis for successful prediction.
n Fruitfulness — A theory should generate a variety of new hypotheses.
n Parsimony — Other things being equal, a simpler theory is preferable to a more
complicated one.
Of these, predictive power is perhaps the acid test of a theory. Two points should be made,
however. The first is that the theory selected for use here is seen as one way of approach-
ing administrative behavior. Other theories may have greater value and their development
and utilization should, of course, be encouraged. On the other hand, and this is the second
point, the criteria used appear to be useful in providing a general assessment of theory.

This is especially true when theoretical formulations may be deficient in obvious respects,
as has been undeniably the case with several approaches in administration.

The use of product design and development processes across multiple companies is referred
to as Collaborative Product Development (CPD). Usually this calls for transparent integra-
tion across heterogeneous computer center architecture and system/application system plat-
forms. CPD can improve product launch success and, therefore, have an impact on reducing
cost and speeding up time to market. Mandatory benefits of a CPD should include sharing
specifications, test results, design changes, and the use of online prototyping, and customer
feedback processing. Shared and integrated information may realize reduced development
costs and time due to tightly integrating and streamlining communication channels.
Every product development process should ask:
1. What are the needs of the customer?
2. How large of a potential market is there for the product?
3. What is the perceived product modification cycle and projected half-life for the product?
Then using the SCM data flows, the following chain of events can be conducted: planning
for design, the actual manufacturing process for the product, and for producing the product.
Rather than having each of the functional and business components corporately organized
as a disconnected network of independent islands of knowledge, CPDs offer an architectural
supportive of product design and development, as well as new product development. The
end result of the CPDs is the development, processing, and customer delivery that gets the
product to the customer cheaply, timely, and with high quality and, simultaneously, main-

45.1 i ntroduction
Whether a research study is labeled as applied or theoretical is immaterial. What is impor-
tant is that the study be precise and accurate. A research field is not a collection of diverse
topical areas; but it is a discipline. Since it is a discipline then researchers should possess a
familiarity with axiomatic approaches and a proficiency at formal reasoning. Formalism often
enables researchers to convey ideas or results with precision and clarity.
45.2 s ample s tudy
Study Discovery of Functional and Approximate Functional Dependencies in Relational
Databases available at http://www.emis.de/journals/HOA/JAMDS/7/149.pdf. This study
develops the foundation for a simple, yet efficient method for uncovering functional and
approximate functional dependencies in relational databases.
1
The technique is based upon
the mathematical theory of partitions done over a relation’s row identifiers. Using a level-
wise algorithm, the minimal nontrivial functional dependencies can be found using com-
putations conducted on integers. Therefore, the required operations on partitions are both
simple and fast. Additionally, the row identifiers provide the added advantage of nominally
identifying the exceptions to approximate functional dependencies, which can be used effec-
tively in practical data mining applications.
45.3 a xiomatic d evelopment as a r esearch m ethod
Assume that you are a new employee for a globally sized company and put in charge of
designing the corporate database. How will you convince the management and stakeholders
that your database is valid and reliable? Clearly, this cannot be achieved empirically since,
for all practical matters, the database appears to us as infinitely large. Thanks to the axiom-
atic method, this task can be resolved. Relational database design through the use of formal
semantics can be rigorously and ruthlessly specified.
If you implement a software package for electronic mail and are unfamiliar with the effects
of flow, then your package will never run. Axiomatic development in general, as illustrated
by the article discussed, forces the researcher to face and deal with questions as fundamental
and diverse as:
n ALGORITHM EXISTENCE
• Does there exist a solution for a given problem?
n ALGORITHM SPECIFICATION
• How should the algorithms be specified?
n EXPRESSIVE POWER
• Does one method of specifying algorithms have greater expressive power than a
second; that is, can more algorithms be specified using it?

The axiomatic development of the relational data model is a perfect example of theoretical
research that has had a major impact on real world problem solving and applications. The
next section will introduce the foundation for the axiomatic development of the relational
data model. A section then follows on strong relations. Finally, there is a section on strong
inter-related relations.
45.4 d efinition for the r elational d ata m odel
Reconsider the earlier problem where you have been hired by the airline company in the
world. The company’s corporate assignment is to design and implement a new world-wide
corporate data base. How will you convince the corporate board that your data base is
valid and reliable? Many individuals would choose to run a pilot study on query and data

manipulation processing using a sub-data base for which the correct answers were known.
Then tests are passed if the processing generates the known answers. But this pilot testing
is totally inaccurate. What if an extreme sub-data base was chosen? What if the query and/

that any data base, which can be practically viewed as an infinitely large data base, can not
be empirically tested.
The relational data model has been axiomatically derived and, as a result, offers the capabil-
ity to test the criteria of goodness of a proposed relational data base design. This approach
clearly enables the designer to defend his data base design to the corporate board members.

1. A relation is a uniquely named two dimensional table.
2. An attribute is a uniquely named, within the definition of the relation, column of the
relation.
3. The named relation and the set of attributes for a relation is called a schema.
4. The rows of a relation are called tuples. A tuple has one component for each attri-
bute of the relation.
5. A design is composed of one or more relational schema.
6. The set of schemas for the relations in a design is called a database schema.
7. The relational model requires that each component of each tuple be atomic, they
must be single valued.
8. Each attribute of a relation is a domain; that is a particular data type.
9. If an assigned value to an attribute X forces another attribute Y to have a specific
value, then X functionally determines Y and is denoted as X → Y. X → Y is called a
functional dependency.
10. A set of two or more attributes is a key for a relation R if:
a. those attributes functionally determine all other attributes of the relation, and
b. no proper subset of the set of attributes functionally determines all other attri-
butes of R, this minimal set of attributes is called a primary key.
Practically speaking the values assigned to tuples in a relation are facts, while the func-
tional dependencies associated with the relation represent information. This becomes read-
ily apparent when one is exposed to Armstrong’s Axioms [found in Database Systems the
Complete Book, by Hector Garcia-Molina, Jeffrey D. Ullman, and Jennifer Widom, Prentice
Hall, Inc.], statements that are true without proof.

What is meant by a strong relation? Two examples are [found in Database Systems the Complete
Book, by Hector Garcia-Molina, Jeffrey D. Ullman, and Jennifer Widom, Prentice Hall, Inc.]:
A relation is Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) if and only if whenever there is a nontrivial
functional dependency X → Y where Y ⊆ R, then it is the case that X is a superkey for R.
A relation R is in third normal form (3NF) if whenever X → Y is a nontrivial functional
dependency, either X is a superkey or Y is a member of some key for R.

45.8 t he a xiomatic m ethod as a t ool for r esearch
The major value of the axiomatic method is its use as a tool for opening up vast new domains
for investigation. Use of the axiomatic method in teaching affords the student a chance to
experience the thrill of creating concepts and to glimpse the inherent beauty of the field
under study. The axiomatic method not only encourages researchers to develop their own
creative powers, but sometimes leads to the invention of new methods not previously con-
ceived. A great merit of the axiomatic approach, as illustrated in both the sample study article
and the discussion in previous sections, is that it admits the possibility of a mixture of deduc-
tive and empirical thinking. Axiomatic development is simply the application of the scientific
method to problems classically recognized as purely theoretical.

45.10 s emantic d ata m odels p roject
Semantic data models have emerged from a requirement for more expressive conceptual
data models. Current generation data models lack direct support for relationships, data
abstraction, inheritance, constraints, unstructured objects, and the dynamic properties of an
application. Although the need for data models with richer semantics is widely recognized,
no single approach has won general acceptance.
a. What are the generic properties of semantic data models?
b. Present a representative selection of models that have been proposed since the
mid-1970s.
c. Offer guidelines for the comparison of models.
d. Discuss the future directions in the population of conceptual data modeling.
45.11 e xtended r elational m odels
Historically, there has been a need within the database community to extend the relational
model to accommodate more real-world knowledge. It is interesting that many of the required
extensions cannot be accommodated by the model theoretic paradigm for relational databases.
a. Perform a topical search on the large number of proposals that have been conducted
in response to this need.
b. How can one begin to compare these proposals? Discuss the limitations you discover
in your topical search. Why should one believe that the definitions for these proposals
are correct or complete?
